source.title: From Topology to Retrieval: Decoding Embedding Spaces with Unified Signatures
source.authors: Florian Rottach; William Rudman; Bastian Rieck; Harrisen Scells; Carsten Eickhoff

record.file_problem: None noted; the full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study directly compares global embedding-space similarity across model sizes and families, and concludes that family-related factors dominate over scale. This refines and challenges scale-driven convergence.
record.gate_note: Rows cover the paper’s global representational-similarity analyses using UTS and CKA. Retrieval-performance prediction, retrievability bias, and predictions of model attributes are not rows because they do not measure representational convergence. Cited findings from prior work are not recorded as results.
record.test_reason: The study explicitly tests whether text-embedding geometry converges with scale, using UTS global-signature distances across 27 models and 11 datasets plus a CKA comparison. It argues that model family, not size, drives similarity, a direct argument against V1. The measure differs from the original: UTS compares summary statistics of each space rather than paired-input kernel alignment.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that global embedding-space geometry clusters by model family, and that architecture and training data shape similarity more than scale, challenging scale-driven (Platonic) global convergence. Their conclusion also states that models of the same family and size category share the most similar topology, so size is not irrelevant.
record.recipe_differences: Uses multidimensional topological signatures normalized across embedding spaces and Manhattan distances, rather than the original Platonic Representation Hypothesis measurement approach; also compares results with CKA.
record.method_sensitivity: The qualitative family-related alignment pattern is reported as similar under UTS and CKA. The paper does not report systematic sensitivity tests of the convergence result across metric settings or input distributions.
record.problems: The comparison is restricted to English text embedding models for retrieval tasks. The scale analysis uses size categories and does not establish a capability-matched scaling trend. The authors do not causally isolate architecture, training data, and objectives; no uncertainty estimates are stated for the reported global-similarity comparisons.
record.rows_left_out: No additional global-convergence results were reported in a form requiring separate rows. Other UTS results concern retrieval prediction, retrievability bias, or model-property classification, not convergence.

untested.parts: Alignment versus measured capability or performance. Cross-modal or non-text models. Paired-input alignment measures such as mutual k-NN, as in the original; UTS compares only global summary statistics.
All parts. The seeds are resampling seeds for computing signatures, not training seeds.
All parts; no mapping, stitching or relative-representation experiments.
All parts; no feature- or circuit-level analysis.
Metric hyperparameters (e.g., number of neighbours), input-distribution or out-of-distribution shifts, and whether the scale trend specifically changes with the metric.
A plateau with scale, and a causal separation of training data from objectives or architecture.

missing.what: Numeric intra- and inter-family UTS distances (diagonal 0.15–0.62; off-diagonal up to 1.24) are not recorded in R1.
UMAP of signatures shows clustering by family and a general clustering by size that correlates with architecture (larger models are decoders), a confound for any scale reading.

Different families have different topological drivers of similarity (e.g., Qwen has high effective rank, Gemini is driven by clustering). Convergence is attributed mainly to density and dimensionality descriptors.
The size–effective-rank relation is largely explained by embedding dimension, which confounds size effects on geometry.

record.verdict_notes: The original record's V7 limits_scope label described untested parts (causal isolation), not a qualifying result, so it was dropped and moved to untested. UTS distance compares vectors of global descriptors (intrinsic dimension, isotropy, homology and so on), not representations of paired inputs. Two spaces could match in signature without being aligned in the original's sense, which weakens the bearing on V1. Peer-review status was not checked here.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not test whether alignment rises with measured capability, or isolate independently trained models matched for architecture, data, and objectives. It studies global topology of text embedding models, not representations across arbitrary modalities.
No paired image-caption vision/language representations or cross-modal alignment are tested.
Although signatures are generated with three seeds, the paper does not report whether independently initialized networks learn shared features or subspaces.
No mapping, stitching, relative-representation, or unpaired interchangeability experiment is reported.
The study does not test recurrence of interpretable features, neurons, or circuits.

The study compares UTS and CKA at the level of global similarity patterns. It does not systematically vary metric settings, neighborhood size, or input distributions, and does not test out-of-distribution inputs.

The study reports family-related clustering and says architecture and training data matter, but does not establish causal effects of shared training data or objectives, quantify a plateau, or compare alignment with a common model of reality.

rows.subject: 27 text embedding models (aggregate)
rows.size_stated: Models span the sizes listed in Table 3; no aggregate size stated.
rows.operation_detail: Compared global UTS signatures using Manhattan distance; pairwise model distances were averaged across datasets.

conditions.value: 11 retrieval datasets; distances averaged across datasets

rows.measure: Global UTS distance between embedding-space signatures
rows.value: Intra-family distances are consistently lower; BERT-based families (BGE, T5, GTE) cluster tightly, as do Qwen and OpenAI models.
rows.locator: Results, “Global topologies cluster by model family”; Figures 6 and 12
rows.note: The reported family-level clustering indicates similarity within families, not broad convergence across different families. The authors say architecture and training data are more influential than scale.
rows.check: Family clustering does not measure change with scale, so it bears on V7 (shared architecture and data explain similarity), not directly on V1. numbers_found is empty although Fig. 6 gives values. Intra-family distances are BGE 0.24, T5 0.15, GTE 0.27, OpenAI 0.37, Qwen 0.45 and E5 0.62. Inter-family distances reach 1.24 (OpenAI–GTE). The family-to-alignment link is correlational.

rows.subject: 27 text embedding models (aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Compared global UTS distances across model-size categories.

conditions.value: small, medium, and large parameter-count categories

rows.baseline: Distances between models of the same size category
rows.value: Models of the same size are more similar; large and small models are most different.
rows.note: The text states the qualitative pattern; Figure 13 displays the category distances. Same-size similarity does not show increasing alignment across scale, and the largest and smallest groups are reported as most different.
rows.check: The text reports only that same-size models are more similar and that large and small models differ most. It does not report that large models are closer to each other than small models are. The Fig. 13 diagonal values are garbled in the text but appear similar (roughly 0.70 vs 0.71), so there is no sign of greater convergence among the largest models. Numbers should be read from the figure.

source_check.correct: state: cannot_determine. Same-size models are more similar than different-size models; large and small models differ most. This qualitative comparison does not establish the trend in within-category alignment with increasing scale.
source_check.locator_found: Section 3.6, Topological clustering; Appendix E.2; Figure 13.
source_check.problem: The recorded category-separation result does not by itself establish an absent V1 scaling effect.

rows.subject: 27 text embedding models (aggregate)
rows.size_stated: Models span the sizes listed in Table 3; no aggregate size stated.
rows.operation_detail: Compared model-family alignment patterns measured with CKA against the UTS-based comparison.
rows.measure: Average representational alignment between model families
rows.value: The authors report a similar pattern with CKA: architecture and training data play a significant role in alignment.
rows.note: The qualitative family-related pattern persists under CKA rather than disappearing under this alternative similarity measure.
rows.check: The state is absent for V6: the family-level pattern does not change between UTS and CKA (Fig. 12 gives CKA-derived family distances of about 0.14–0.43). For V7, CKA also shows family-driven alignment. CKA was not applied to the size grouping, so metric dependence of the scale result itself is not tested.

relationships.condition: English text embedding models (0.02B–8B, encoders and decoders) on 11 retrieval datasets, under UTS global-signature distance
relationships.reason: Same-size grouping shows no greater similarity among large models, which differ most from small models (R2). Families such as Qwen cluster despite their size spread. Only qualitative text and a figure are given.
relationships.display_finding: Large models show no greater within-size similarity and differ most from small models, while families such as Qwen cluster across sizes.
